definition: A rich, image-heavy section that appears on an Amazon product page below the bullet points, with branded modules like comparison charts, lifestyle images, and a brand story. It is only available to sellers who have completed Amazon Brand Registry. It helps build trust and lift the percentage of viewers who buy.

A measure of how much you spend on Amazon ads compared to the sales those ads generate, shown as a percentage. For example, spending £20 on ads to make £100 in sales is a 20% ACOS. A lower number means your advertising is more efficient; a common rule is to keep ACOS below your profit margin.

A page in Seller Central where Amazon scores how well you follow its rules and keep customers happy. It flags policy warnings, performance problems, and complaints. If key numbers cross a limit, Amazon can suspend your account, so the course says to check it regularly and fix issues fast.

A large online marketplace where businesses buy products in bulk directly from overseas (mostly Chinese) manufacturers. The course deliberately avoids it at the start, preferring local UK shelf and wholesale sourcing until a product is proven.

Amazon's own video-call app, used in the browser without installing anything. New sellers use it for the identity verification video call during account sign-up, where a verifier checks your face against your ID.

When Amazon itself is the seller on a listing, often shown as 'Sold by Amazon'. The course advises avoiding building bundles around products Amazon sells directly, because Amazon's pricing is unpredictable and it tends to undercut third-party sellers.

Amazon's official review programme where you give away free units of your product to trusted, Amazon-vetted reviewers who then leave honest reviews. It is available to brand-registered sellers and is used to build review credibility on a new listing. You have no control over what reviewers say.

The average amount a customer spends in a single purchase. Selling bundles raises this number because the customer buys several items at once instead of one, which makes Amazon's flat per-item fees a smaller share of each sale and leaves more profit.

A unique 10-character code Amazon assigns to every product in its catalogue. Listing against an existing ASIN means joining other sellers competing for the same Buy Box; creating a unique bundle earns a brand-new ASIN that only you sell on.

A type of Amazon pay-per-click ad where Amazon automatically chooses which search terms to show your product against, based on your listing. It is run first to discover which keywords actually convert, which you then move into more targeted manual campaigns.

An Amazon feature that automatically raises and lowers your price in response to competitors. The course recommends leaving it off for new listings because it tends to race prices to the bottom; if used later, you must set hard minimum and maximum price limits first.

Also called backend search terms: keywords you enter in a hidden field of your listing that customers never see but Amazon's search engine still reads. They let you target spelling variants and extra phrases that did not fit in your title or bullets. The field holds about 250 characters and should not repeat words already in your title.

A standard UK bank transfer method for moving money between accounts, commonly used to pay supplier invoices. The course mentions paying wholesale suppliers by BACS or card once you receive a proforma invoice.

The date by which a consumable product is at its best quality. The course warns that stock close to its best-before date is risky to send into Amazon, because it can become unsellable while sitting in the warehouse, especially during the busy Q4 period.

A set of data reports inside Seller Central available to brand-registered sellers. It shows insights like what customers search for and how they shop, helping you make better listing and advertising decisions.

An Amazon programme that proves you own a brand (it requires a pending or registered trademark) and gives you control and protection over your listings. It unlocks A+ Content, Brand Story, the Vine review programme, Sponsored Brands ads, and the ability to report hijackers. The course saves this for after a product has proven it sells.
A branded module on your Amazon product page that tells customers who your brand is and what it stands for. Like A+ Content, it is only available once you have completed Amazon Brand Registry.

A dedicated mini multi-page website inside Amazon showcasing all of a brand's products, available to brand-registered sellers. Big brands use these to pull search traffic toward their own products; the course also treats their presence as a sign a brand aggressively controls its space and is best avoided by a new seller.

Amazon's ranking of how well a product sells within its category, updated hourly. A lower number means more sales (rank #1 is the top seller). Sellers use it to gauge real demand before sourcing a product.

The five short, scannable statements near the top of an Amazon listing, next to the main image. Each should lead with a benefit and then back it up with a feature, kept under about 200 characters. Most buyers decide here whether to add the item to their basket, since few read the full description.

Two or more products (or a multipack of the same product) combined and sold together as a single new listing. Because the combination is unique, it gets its own ASIN that only you sell on, letting you avoid price competition. Bundling is the core strategy taught in this course.

The course's final checklist used to decide whether a researched product is worth actually buying and selling as a bundle. Each criterion either passes or fails, and a bundle that fails several is dropped. It is the last gate before spending money.

The box on a product page with the 'Add to Basket' and 'Buy Now' buttons. When several sellers offer the same item, only one wins the Buy Box at a time and gets most of the sales. Only Professional-plan sellers are eligible, and owning a unique bundle ASIN means you hold 100% of its Buy Box with no competition.

A free, beginner-friendly online design tool. The course uses it to add clean, readable text and icons on top of product images (since AI tools often produce garbled text) and to make a simple brand wordmark. It includes templates sized correctly for Amazon listing images.

The fixed number of units a wholesale supplier sells a product in, such as a case of 24. Distributors price and ship by the case rather than single items, so you usually have to buy at least one full case when going wholesale.

A shipment method where you send many identical units grouped inside inner cartons, rather than individually. The course uses 'Individual products' mode for early bundle shipments and notes case-pack is a later optimisation once you ship 50+ identical units at a time.

A wholesale warehouse where small businesses pay and take goods away themselves, often in small case quantities (examples include Bestway and Booker). The course highlights these, which supply local corner shops and mini-markets, as an accessible source of ongoing stock.

A keyword-research tool inside Helium 10 that does a 'reverse-ASIN lookup': you enter a competitor's product and it shows all the search keywords that product ranks for, ranked by search volume, so you can build your own keyword list.

The official document proving your limited company legally exists, issued when you register it. You receive it (usually within about 24 hours) along with your company number after paying the registration fee.

When a customer disputes a charge through their bank or card provider and the money is forcibly reversed. Amazon briefly holds some of your sale funds in reserve partly to cover possible chargebacks and returns before paying you.

The shipment status meaning Amazon's warehouse has physically scanned and received your boxes. Your inventory only goes live for sale once it is fully checked in, which can take several days after delivery.

A small add-on you install into the Chrome web browser to add extra features. In this course it refers mainly to the free Helium 10 extension, which overlays sales and ranking data directly onto Amazon search pages.
The direct cost of the products you sell, meaning what you pay your supplier per unit. It is one of the main deductions from your sale price (alongside Amazon fees) when working out net profit.

The UK government body where limited companies are registered. You set up your Ltd company here (for around £12-£50), choosing a company name, registered address, at least one director, and a SIC code describing your business activity.

A bundle made of two genuinely different products that solve the same problem together, like shampoo paired with matching conditioner. The customer benefit is curation, someone has picked the right combination for them. These are harder to design but more defensible than simple multi-packs.

The truthful safety and regulatory statements you must enter when creating a listing, such as whether a product is hazardous or what country it came from. Getting these wrong can block your shipment or flag your account, so the course stresses answering honestly and accurately.

The percentage of people who view your listing and then actually buy. A high conversion rate signals to Amazon that your product is worth showing, which improves your search ranking. Good images, reviews, price, and copy all lift it.
The UK tax a limited company pays on its profits. After registering your Ltd company you must register for Corporation Tax and keep basic bookkeeping to report it.

The country where a product was actually manufactured (not where it was packed), which you must declare on the listing. It must match what is printed on the product packaging, or it can cause compliance problems.

The percentage of shoppers who see your listing in search results or an ad and then click on it. A strong main image and price are the biggest drivers, which in turn signal relevance to Amazon's algorithm.

A unit of volume (roughly 30cm x 30cm x 30cm) Amazon uses to measure and bill the storage space your inventory takes up in its warehouses each month. The more cubic feet your stock occupies, the higher your monthly storage fee.

The machine Amazon uses in its warehouses to automatically re-measure the size and weight of every box and unit you send in. If your declared dimensions are smaller than what the Cubiscan measures, you get bumped into a higher (more expensive) size tier, so always measure your packed, polybagged bundle.

The payout Amazon sends to your bank account for your sales, after deducting its fees. Until you verify your deposit bank account and complete the tax interview, sales can accrue but never disburse, leaving your money stuck in 'Pending'.

A company that supplies a brand's products in bulk to shops and resellers, usually within a specific country. The course teaches you to find a brand's UK distributor (often named on the back of the packaging) and buy wholesale from them to cut your costs.

A bright label (usually reading 'DO NOT SEPARATE - SOLD AS SET') applied to any bundle that contains more than one physical unit sold under a single SKU, such as a 3-pack. It tells Amazon's warehouse staff to keep the units together and sell them as one item. It is mandatory for multi-unit bundles.
A UK parcel courier that, along with UPS, is one of Amazon's partnered carriers. You can choose it inside the Send to Amazon wizard to ship stock to Amazon at a discounted, Amazon-negotiated rate.

A brand of thermal label printer suitable for printing FNSKU product labels at home. Thermal printers print using heat instead of ink, making label printing faster and cheaper at volume, though they are not required to start.

A standard product barcode used in Europe and the UK (a type of GTIN), found on most retail packaging. Because the course's bundles are new combinations without their own barcode, you apply for a GTIN exemption instead of buying one.

Amazon's service where you send your products to Amazon's warehouses and Amazon handles storage, picking, packing, shipping, customer service, and returns for you. You handle the buying and strategy; Amazon handles the physical work, and FBA products automatically get the Prime badge.

The alternative to FBA where you store your own stock and handle all packing, postage, returns, and customer service yourself. Listings don't get the Prime badge and show slower delivery, so they sell worse. The course deliberately avoids FBM.

When Amazon changes the fees it charges sellers, which it does periodically. The course builds in a margin buffer (aiming for 30%+ and £5+ net per unit) so an unexpected fee increase does not wipe out a product's profit.

The course's minimum-profitability standard: a bundle is only sourced if it clears every target at once, roughly £5+ net profit per unit, 30%+ margin, 60+ sales per month, and fast inventory turnover. If any metric fails, the bundle is skipped.

The unique barcode-and-text label Amazon generates for your specific product, encoding which seller, product, and condition it is. Every individual unit you send to FBA needs one, applied over any existing retail barcode so Amazon's scanners read only your code.

An Amazon warehouse where your products are stored, then picked, packed, and shipped to customers. When you sell through FBA you send your stock here, and Amazon decides which centre(s) receive it, sometimes splitting a shipment across several.

The flat charge Amazon takes for physically picking, packing, and shipping each of your items to the customer. It is based on the product's size and weight, not its price, so smaller and lighter bundles cost less to fulfil.
Stock at Amazon that is in good condition and available to be sold to customers. When a returned item comes back undamaged, Amazon puts it back into fulfillable inventory to sell again.

A product category that is restricted, so you must get Amazon's approval (be 'ungated') before you can sell in it. Examples include supplements and medical items. New sellers should stick to open (ungated) categories like Beauty, Home, Pet, and Toys.

Listing a product under the accepted brand name 'Generic' instead of a trademarked brand, which lets you launch and test a bundle without owning a trademark, barcode, or Brand Registry. The course uses this for early validation, switching to a registered brand only once a product proves itself.
The umbrella term for the standard product identification barcodes (such as UPC and EAN) that most products carry. Amazon normally requires one to create a listing.

Amazon's free permission to list a product without a standard barcode, which is how you list unique bundles or generic-brand products. The application is photo-based: you show the product and prove your brand name is permanently part of the packaging. Approval usually arrives within a few days.

Products classified as potentially dangerous to store or ship, such as aerosols, batteries, or flammable liquids. You must declare these honestly on your listing; misdeclaring them is an account-health failure when Amazon detects it on arrival.

A bright warning sticker required on any outer box that weighs over 15kg, telling carrier and warehouse staff to lift it as a two-person job. Boxes over 23kg must be split into two. Shipping a heavy box without it can get it refused and trigger a non-compliance fee.

A popular suite of software tools for Amazon sellers. The course uses its free Chrome extension (especially the X-Ray feature) for product research and its keyword tools (Cerebro, Magnet) later for marketing. It removes a lot of guesswork.

A seller who attaches their own (often counterfeit or cheaper) offer to your product listing without permission, stealing sales and risking your reputation. Brand Registry lets you report and remove hijackers.
The UK government tax authority. Sellers must keep their tax affairs up to date with HMRC; the course references it when discussing the Amazon tax interview and registering a company.

The simple code used to format text on web pages. Amazon's description field flattens normal text into one block, so wrapping it in a few basic HTML tags preserves paragraphs and bold text. The course uses a free one-click tool to do this, so you don't need to know any code.

A batch of your products that you send into an Amazon fulfilment centre to be stocked and sold. You create an inbound shipment plan in Seller Central telling Amazon what you are sending, how much, and from where, then ship it to the assigned warehouse.

Amazon's basic seller plan with no monthly fee but a charge of about £0.75 per item sold, and no Buy Box eligibility, ads, or ungating. The course recommends starting here during account verification, then upgrading to Professional once your first stock is checked in.

A product image that combines a photo with short text callouts and icons to highlight features or benefits (such as 'dishwasher-safe' or '24 pieces'). It communicates key selling points visually to shoppers who skim rather than read.
How long your stock has been sitting in Amazon's warehouse. Older inventory costs more in storage fees and can trigger penalties after 180 days, so sellers monitor it and aim to sell stock quickly.

A score Amazon gives your account for how efficiently you manage stock. It influences your storage limits, so a poor score can cap how much inventory you can send in. It lives in the Inventory section of Seller Central.
How quickly you sell through your stock. The course targets selling a batch within about 45 days, because slow-moving stock starts incurring long-term storage fees that compound losses.

A tool (browser extension and website) that shows the price history and sales-rank trends of Amazon products over time. The course uses it to check whether a product's price and demand have been stable rather than falling.

A specific word or phrase a customer types into Amazon's search bar, like 'stainless steel cutlery set'. Your listing must contain the keywords your customers actually use, or your product won't appear when they search. Finding and using the right keywords is central to being found.

An email-marketing app commonly used with Shopify stores to send automated emails to customers and build an email list. The course suggests it as a lean add-on when you eventually build your own website.

An account-health metric tracking the percentage of orders you ship late. It only applies to seller-fulfilled (FBM) orders and should stay below 4%. With FBA, Amazon handles shipping so this is not your concern.

The time between placing and paying for an order with a supplier and the stock actually being despatched to you. Knowing a supplier's lead time lets you plan when stock can be sent into Amazon and avoid running out.

The course's core framework, also stated as Lean, Validate, Scale: start small by testing a product with only 5 to 12 units, prove it sells, and only then buy more and grow. It avoids the beginner mistake of spending thousands upfront on stock that might not sell.

A product photo showing the item in real-world use and context (for example a cutlery set on a laid dining table). It helps the customer picture themselves using the product and communicates who it is for. These fill the optional secondary image slots after the main image.

A registered UK business that is legally separate from you as an individual, protecting your personal finances and adding credibility. The course advises forming one (via Companies House) after a product is selling, not on day one, to avoid overcomplicating tax and banking too early.

The product page customers see on Amazon, and also the data record Amazon's search system reads. It includes the title, images, bullets, description, price, and reviews. A good listing must get found by search, get clicked, and get the customer to buy.

A Helium 10 score (0-10), sometimes shown as LQS, rating how well a listing is optimised across title, bullets, images, A+ content, and keywords. The course uses it to spot weak competitors: a category full of low scores is one you can win simply by optimising properly.

When Amazon hides your listing from search and sale, usually because something is missing or breaks a rule (like a bad main image). A suppressed listing earns nothing until you fix the flagged problem.

Extra heavy charges Amazon adds when your stock sits in its warehouse for more than 180 days. They can swallow your profits, which is why the course tests with only a small number of units first instead of buying hundreds.
A keyword-research tool within Helium 10 that generates large lists of related keywords from a seed term. It is one of the paid Helium 10 features used during the marketing stage of the course.

The first, primary photo of your product shown in search results and at the top of your listing. Amazon requires it to be the product alone on a pure white background, filling most of the frame, with no text or props. It is the single biggest driver of whether shoppers click your listing.

An Amazon ad where you personally choose which keywords to bid on, rather than letting Amazon pick. 'Broad' match shows your ad on loosely related searches; 'Exact' match shows it only on your precise winning keywords. Used once an auto campaign reveals which keywords convert.

The portion of a sale's price you keep as profit after all costs and fees, shown as a percentage. For example, £5 net profit on a £20 sale is a 25% margin. The course requires at least 30% so a product still earns money after fee increases, returns, and peak-season storage.

An Amazon service that ships orders you made on other platforms (like eBay or your own website) using your stock already stored in Amazon's warehouses. It lets one inventory pool serve multiple sales channels, though it costs more and ships in Amazon packaging unless you opt out.
A unit measuring the thickness of plastic. Amazon requires polybags used in FBA to be at least 38 microns thick so they are durable enough for warehouse handling.

The smallest amount a wholesale supplier will let you buy in a single order. Suppliers set an MOQ partly to filter out non-serious buyers, so you usually must commit to at least that quantity to open a wholesale relationship.

A bundle made of several of the same item packaged together, such as a 3-pack. It is easy to build because you only source one item, but faces more competition since the idea is obvious. The course favours multipacks for the first few listings.

Search terms you tell Amazon NOT to show your ads against, because they waste money without converting. Adding poor-performing search terms to your negative keyword list is a key part of the weekly PPC review to keep ad spend efficient.

The actual money left in your pocket after every cost is taken out: product cost, Amazon referral and fulfilment fees, prep, returns, and storage. The course tells operators to focus on net profit per unit, not total revenue, because revenue hides costs.

A penalty Amazon charges when your inbound shipment breaks its preparation or labelling rules, for example a missing label or a box weight that doesn't match. Amazon may also charge to fix the problem for you, eating into your profit.
Technology that reads text from a photo or scanned document. Amazon uses it during seller verification to automatically pull your name, address, and date of birth from your uploaded ID documents.

An account-health metric measuring the share of your orders that had a problem (negative feedback, an A-to-z claim, or a chargeback). Amazon requires it to stay below 1%; exceeding it risks suspension.

Search results or sales you get naturally from Amazon's search rankings, without paying for ads. The opposite is paid placement through PPC. Strong listings and keywords earn more organic visibility over time.

A summary of money coming in versus money going out, showing whether a business or product makes a profit. The course says running 'a real P&L' means treating each bundle like a serious business with tracked income and costs, not a casual hobby.
When Amazon transfers your accumulated sales earnings (after fees and reserves) to your bank account. Payouts are typically made about every 14 days rather than immediately after each sale.

A short formal document (also called a POA) you write to Amazon to recover a suspended account or listing. It has three parts: the root cause of the problem, the immediate fix, and the long-term prevention. Keeping it factual and brief works better than long explanations.

A clear plastic bag that each bundle is sealed inside before being sent to Amazon. It must be transparent and at least 38 microns thick, and any bag with an opening 12.5cm or wider needs a printed suffocation warning. The FNSKU label goes on its flattest face.

Amazon advertising where you bid on keywords and only pay when someone clicks your ad. Its main job, per the course, is to teach Amazon what your product is relevant for, which improves your natural search ranking, while you watch ACOS to stay profitable.

The work of getting a unit ready for FBA: polybagging it, applying the FNSKU and any required warning labels, and packing it. 'Inbound shipping and prep' is one of the per-unit costs counted when calculating a bundle's profit.

Amazon's paid membership giving customers fast free delivery plus video, music, and other perks. More than half of UK and US households have it, and members strongly prefer products with the Prime badge, which is why earning that badge (automatic with FBA) is so valuable to sellers.

The small blue 'Prime' mark on a product page showing the item ships fast and free to Prime members and is backed by Amazon. Products fulfilled through FBA get it automatically. It dramatically increases trust and sales, even letting you charge more than non-Prime competitors.

Amazon's big annual sales event (typically in July) with heavy discounts for Prime members. The course notes it as a peak period when warehouses are busy and inbound shipments are received more slowly.

Selling products under your own brand rather than reselling someone else's. The course's later phase moves from generic bundling toward becoming a protected, trademarked private-label brand once a product is proven.

Amazon's paid seller plan (around £25-£30 plus VAT per month) with no per-item fee and full features including Buy Box eligibility, advertising, ungating, and brand tools. It becomes cheaper than the Individual plan once you sell more than about 33 units a month.

A preliminary invoice a supplier sends before an order is fulfilled, showing the total and their payment details so you can pay. Once you pay the proforma, the supplier's lead time to despatch begins.
Evidence, from real sales, that a product idea actually works before you invest heavily in it. The whole lean approach is built around proving the concept with a small test batch first, then scaling.

The October-to-December period covering the holiday shopping rush. Amazon roughly triples its storage fees then to discourage slow-moving stock, and warehouses receive inbound shipments more slowly, so the course warns that thin profit margins can collapse during Q4.

The warehouse stage where Amazon staff unload your inbound box, scan each unit, and check it into your inventory. Your listing only becomes buyable once receiving finishes. The course says to raise a support case if a shipment is stuck in receiving over five working days outside peak season.

The commission Amazon takes from each sale for providing the marketplace and customers, calculated as a percentage of the total price the customer pays. For the everyday categories the course targets, it is a flat 15%, deducted automatically the moment a sale happens.

Money from your sales that Amazon temporarily holds back before paying you, to cover possible returns or chargebacks. Funds sit in this account reserve for a short period rather than landing in your bank instantly after each sale.

Stock that is temporarily unavailable to sell because Amazon is moving it between warehouses or it is tied to a pending customer order awaiting dispatch. It appears as a status alongside 'Available' and 'Inbound' in your inventory view.

The percentage of your sold units that customers send back, calculated as total returns divided by total units sold. A high return rate (from poor-quality bundles or misleading photos) hurts your account health, so sellers monitor it closely.

A keyword-research technique (done in Helium 10's Cerebro) where you enter a competitor's product (its ASIN) and the tool reveals every keyword that product ranks for, so you can target the same searches.

How much profit you make compared to the money you put in, usually as a percentage. The course has you review ROI monthly to make sure each product is genuinely earning a worthwhile return on the cash you spent on stock and ads.
The UK's national postal service. The course mentions dropping self-shipped eBay orders there when you fulfil orders yourself instead of using Amazon's warehouses.
The standard or list price of a product, sometimes shown as a strikethrough next to a discounted price on Amazon. It helps you gauge a product's typical market value when researching.

Another name for Best Seller Rank: Amazon's measure of how well a product sells in its category, with a lower number meaning more sales. The course uses it as a primary signal of whether a product has proven demand.

How fast a product sells, usually expressed as units per day or per month. Higher velocity signals strong demand to Amazon's algorithm and helps your ranking; the course targets at least 60 units a month and validates velocity before committing wholesale money.

A downloadable report in Seller Central showing the actual customer search terms that triggered your ads and whether they converted. It is the basis of the weekly PPC review: you promote good terms and add bad ones to negative keywords.

Amazon's web dashboard for sellers, where you create listings, manage inventory and shipments, set prices, run ads, file support cases, and monitor account health. Once verified, you spend more time here than anywhere else on Amazon.

Amazon's help service for sellers, accessed by opening a support case in Seller Central tied to a specific listing or order. The course notes front-line support is hit and miss and suggests asking to escalate to a senior associate if the first reply is unhelpful.

An alternative way to earn the Prime badge while shipping orders yourself from home, instead of using FBA. The course notes it demands near-perfect delivery performance and strict audits that almost no individual seller can sustain, so it always uses FBA instead.

A free online tool that converts your plain-text product description into the simple HTML formatting (paragraph breaks, bold) that Amazon's description field needs, so your text stays readable instead of collapsing into one block.

The step-by-step wizard in Seller Central used to create an inbound FBA shipment: you confirm the product and units, print FNSKU labels, enter box size and weight, choose a carrier, pay, and print the shipping label at a discounted rate.

Writing your listing using the exact words customers type when searching, so your product appears in their results. On Amazon it simply means putting the right keywords in your title, bullets, and search-terms field. Get it right and you appear on page one; miss it and you're invisible.

The page of results a shopper sees after searching. Big brands' Sponsored Brands ads can dominate the top of this page, so a new seller's product gets buried. Ranking well on the SERP is key to being seen.

A label Amazon generates that identifies your specific inbound shipment, placed on the outer box (usually on the same printout as the carrier label) so the warehouse knows which shipment plan the box belongs to.

The instructions you create in Seller Central telling Amazon what stock you are sending, how many units, where from, and how it will arrive. Amazon uses it to decide which warehouse(s) receive your shipment.

A platform for building your own online store website, used in the course's expansion module. Unlike Amazon ('rented land'), a Shopify store is 'owned land' where you control the customer relationship, email list, pricing, and brand experience.

A code that describes what a UK company does, chosen when registering at Companies House. For FBA selling it is usually 47910 (retail sale via mail order or internet). Picking the wrong one is a common setup mistake.

Amazon's strict classification of a packed item by its dimensions and weight (for example Small Envelope, Standard Parcel), which determines the fulfilment fee. Crossing a tier boundary by even a millimetre bumps you to the next, more expensive tier, so bundles are packed tightly and flat to stay in the smallest tier.

A unique code you assign to identify each distinct product you sell, used to track and manage inventory. Each bundle is one SKU; a multi-unit bundle is still a single SKU sold and shipped as one item. Amazon tracks stock, sales, and labelling by SKU.

An individual who runs a business in their own name without forming a company, the simplest UK business structure. The course recommends starting as a sole trader (selected as 'Individual' on Amazon) and only incorporating a limited company later.

An Amazon ad format that shows your brand logo and several products at the top of search results, available only to brand-registered sellers. Big brands use these to capture the first clicks; the course covers them once you have a registered brand.
An Amazon ad format that targets shoppers on and off Amazon, including retargeting people who viewed your product. It is unlocked alongside other brand advertising tools after Brand Registry.

The most common Amazon ad type, promoting a single product within search results and on product pages. It is the core of the PPC strategy taught in the marketing module and is available on the Professional plan.
A standard colour format for digital images that Amazon requires for listing photos, ensuring colours display consistently. Listing images should be JPEG or PNG in sRGB, at least 1600x1600 pixels.
Running out of inventory at Amazon so your product can't be sold. Stockouts hurt your search ranking and waste your advertising momentum, so the course says to reorder stock before you run out.

The monthly rent Amazon charges for the warehouse space your inventory occupies, measured per cubic foot. They are low most of the year but roughly triple during the Q4 holiday season, and balloon for stock older than 180 days.

Amazon's system that decides where to place your incoming stock, spreading it across different shelves and regional warehouses. This keeps your product physically close to customers everywhere, maximising delivery speed.

Stock sitting in Amazon's warehouse that can't be sold because of a listing problem (for example the listing is inactive or has an error), yet still accrues storage fees. The course's weekly routine includes checking for stranded SKUs so you can fix them and start selling that stock again.

A printed safety warning Amazon requires on any polybag with an opening 12.5cm or wider, alerting people to keep the plastic bag away from babies and children. You can buy bags with it pre-printed or add a separate label, or risk the bundle being rejected at receiving.

When Amazon locks a seller account or listing, freezing inventory and withholding funds, usually over a policy or performance issue. Common triggers include intellectual property complaints, inauthentic-product claims, and linked accounts. Most are reversible with a good Plan of Action.

A short series of questions Amazon asks during setup about your tax status (sole trader, limited company, VAT-registered or not) to generate the correct tax forms. Completing it prevents Amazon withholding a percentage of your payouts for US tax.
A printer that prints labels using heat instead of ink, producing one sticky label at a time. It is an optional alternative to printing FNSKU labels on sheets, useful once you ship frequently.

An independent seller (like you) who sells on Amazon's marketplace, as opposed to Amazon selling the item itself. The Prime badge is what gives a third-party seller's listings a fair chance against Amazon's own and big brands' products.

An extra security step (like a one-time code) some bank cards require to confirm an online payment. During seller sign-up, a card that triggers a 3D Secure prompt can interrupt verification, so the course flags it as something to be ready for.

TikTok's built-in shopping platform where products are sold through short videos and live streams, used in the course's expansion module. It suits cheap, visual, impulse-buy products that demo well in a few seconds.

Legal ownership of your brand name (and/or logo) so no one else can sell under it. In the UK you register it via gov.uk under specific classes (around £170 for one class, taking 8-12 weeks). A pending or registered trademark is required to join Amazon Brand Registry.

A category of goods or services you register a trademark under (for example Class 21 for kitchenware, Class 25 for clothing). You file under the class(es) matching your products, and each extra class adds to the cost, so choose carefully before submitting.
A sturdy cardboard box made with two layers of corrugated material (also called double-walled), recommended for the outer shipping box so your bundles survive carrier handling without crushing.

An extra login security layer (also called 2SV) requiring a code from an authenticator app or SMS on top of your password. The course calls enabling it the single most important first-hour task, since a hijacked seller account can have its funds drained.

Getting Amazon's approval to sell in a restricted (gated) category or brand that is locked by default. It often requires proof such as wholesale invoices, is only available on the Professional plan, and new sellers usually avoid gated categories until ready.

Returned or damaged stock at Amazon that can't be sold again, for example because the packaging is torn or opened. Amazon marks it unfulfillable and lets you recall it to your home address to inspect or salvage.

The profit and loss of a single sale: sale price minus supplier cost, referral fee, FBA fee, and prep, leaving net profit per unit. It is the most important number in the business; if it is healthy and repeatable, the business scales well. Revenue alone is treated as a misleading vanity figure.

A standard product barcode (a type of GTIN) used mainly in North America and found on most retail packaging. The course's bundles don't have their own UPC, so you apply for a GTIN exemption instead of buying one.

A global parcel courier that, along with DPD, is one of Amazon's UK partnered carriers. You can select it inside the Send to Amazon wizard to ship boxes to the fulfilment centre at a discounted rate, including drop-off at UPS Access Points.

A personal tax reference number issued by the UK tax authority (HMRC). It can come up during Amazon's seller verification, and the course notes it's a detail people commonly forget on the verification call.

A UK sales tax added to many goods and services, including the Professional plan's monthly fee. Suppliers may also ask for your VAT number when setting up a wholesale account, and your VAT status comes up in Amazon's tax interview.
Packing material such as kraft paper or air pillows used to fill empty space inside a shipping box so the contents don't move and get damaged in transit. Amazon dislikes loose foam peanuts.

A measure based on a package's size (the space it takes up) rather than its actual weight, used to work out shipping and fulfilment costs. A bulky but light item can cost more to ship, so the course advises choosing and packing bundles to be compact.

Buying products in bulk directly from a brand's supplier or distributor at below-retail prices for resale, backed by proper business-to-business invoices. The course uses retail to validate a product, then switches to wholesale to cut costs by 30-50% and turn a tested bundle into a long-running profit engine.

An official business-to-business invoice from a verified wholesaler showing your business name and the bulk quantity bought. Unlike a retail shop receipt, it satisfies Amazon's authenticity and compliance checks and can unlock restricted categories.

A simple logo made just of your brand name in a chosen typeface, rather than an elaborate graphic. The course advises a clean, cheap wordmark (via Canva, Looka, or Fiverr) for a new brand instead of an expensive custom logo.

A feature of the free Helium 10 Chrome extension that overlays estimated monthly sales, revenue, Best Seller Rank, review counts, and listing quality scores directly onto any Amazon search page. It lets you size up a whole market at a glance, though its estimates are approximate.
